evidence.limitations: This worker was assigned only the Go language shard; scores for other languages are produced by sibling workers under the same frozen rubric definitions reproduced here. Raw popularity/index-count indicators were used only as one declared, caveated input within D5 of the package-management metric, not as a standalone proxy for either metric.
evidence.methodology_note: Frozen rubric defined before scoring; identical dimension weights are intended to apply unchanged to all 10 languages. This work unit measures only the Go-assigned cells. Each metric decomposes into 5 equally-weighted (0-20) dimensions summing to a 0-100 normalized score. Snapshot date: 2026-09-22.

citations.claim: Go ships a single official toolchain with an active, frequent release/patch cadence including recent security and bug-fix point releases.
citations.support: go1.27.1 (released 2026-09-01) includes fixes to cgo, the compiler, the runtime, the go fix command, and the database/sql, debug/elf, encoding/json, net/http, os, simd, and simd/archsimd packages. Go 1.26.0 is a major release of Go.

citations.claim: Go 1.26 was a major, on-schedule release continuing the standard six-month cadence.
citations.support: The latest Go release, version 1.26, arrives in February 2026, six months after Go 1.25.

citations.claim: go vet is Go's official, built-in static analyzer.
citations.support: go vet is Go's official static analyzer. It examines code for suspicious constructs that are likely bugs.

citations.claim: go fix (rewritten in Go 1.26) builds on the same official analysis framework as go vet, extending first-party static-analysis tooling.
citations.support: The rewritten go fix command builds atop the exact same Go analysis framework as go vet.

citations.claim: golangci-lint is the de facto standard third-party meta-linter, bundling 100+ linters with parallel execution and caching, widely used in professional CI pipelines.
citations.support: It runs over 100 linters together with parallel execution + result caching, and you can centrally manage “which ones to enable” using a configuration file like .golangci.yml.

citations.claim: staticcheck is regarded as the gold standard of third-party Go static analysis, in long-term active maintenance.
citations.support: staticcheck represents the gold standard of Go static analysis.

citations.claim: pprof and trace are built-in official profiling tools distributed with the Go toolchain.
citations.support: go vet · golangci-lint · staticcheck · godoc · pkgsite · delve · pprof · stringer · mockgen · gopls · goimports

citations.claim: Delve, the standard Go debugger, is a third-party tool (installed via go install) that integrates with mainstream editors.
citations.support: Delve integrates with VS Code's debug panel, so you can set breakpoints and inspect state visually without touching the CLI.

rubric: D1 (0-20): Official compiler/build toolchain availability, cross-platform support, release/versioning discipline
D2 (0-20): Official code formatter shipped with the toolchain
D3 (0-20): Static analysis / linting: built-in analyzer plus maturity of the surrounding linter ecosystem
D4 (0-20): Test runner integration (unit tests, benchmarks, coverage, race detection) built into the toolchain
D5 (0-20): Debugger and profiler product maturity (first- or third-party, IDE integration)
metric.core_tooling_availability_quality.scoring_rationale: Go scores near-ceiling because build/format/vet/test/profiling are first-party and bundled in a single `go` command with a disciplined, frequent release/patch cadence (D1=20). gofmt is a universally adopted official formatter (D2=20, well-established, no counter-evidence found). D3 is capped below 20 because deep static analysis beyond go vet (staticcheck, golangci-lint) is mature but third-party rather than bundled. D4 is capped slightly below 20 because `go test` is built-in and highly capable but some advanced assertion/mocking ergonomics still rely on third-party libraries. D5 is capped further because the standard debugger (Delve) is third-party, even though profiling (pprof/trace) is first-party and excellent.

citations.claim: Go modules, managed via the built-in go mod tooling, are the official first-party dependency management system.
citations.support: The Go module system was introduced in Go 1.11 and is the official dependency management solution for Go.

citations.claim: Since Go 1.13 the go command authenticates every downloaded module by default against an auditable, tamper-evident checksum database.
citations.support: Since Go 1.13, the go command by default downloads and authenticates modules using the Go checksum database.

citations.claim: The checksum database is built on a Merkle-tree transparent log designed to make tampering detectable, and the go command verifies inclusion/consistency proofs before trusting go.sum entries.
citations.support: The checksum database is served by sum.golang.org, and is built on a Transparent Log (or “Merkle tree”) of hashes backed by Trillian.

citations.claim: go.sum plus the checksum database is explicitly designed to guarantee repeatable builds and detect unexpected or malicious changes.
citations.support: The go command tries to authenticate every downloaded module, checking that the bits downloaded for a specific module version today match bits downloaded yesterday.

citations.claim: Google's Go team operates official production-grade module mirror, index, and checksum services underpinning the default dependency workflow.
citations.support: The Go team is providing the following services run by Google: a module mirror for accelerating Go module downloads, an index for discovering new modules, and a global go.sum database for authenticating module content.

citations.claim: pkg.go.dev, the official package documentation/discovery site, sources its data directly from the official module proxy.
citations.support: Data for the site is downloaded from proxy.golang.org.

citations.claim: Go 1.18 introduced first-party multi-module workspaces (go.work) allowing simultaneous local development across modules without publishing intermediate versions or replace directives.
citations.support: Go 1.18 introduced workspaces to solve exactly this problem.

citations.claim: Workspace-aware vendoring (go work vendor) extends single-module vendoring to multi-module workspaces for reproducible, network-independent builds.
citations.support: The go work vendor command creates a vendor directory that includes all dependencies required by every module in the workspace.

citations.claim: Interaction between per-module vendoring and workspace vendoring has documented rough edges/ambiguities that required explicit design proposals to resolve.
citations.support: We originally didn't support vendoring of a workspace to simplify the implementation of workspaces, but there's recently been demand by users of vendoring who want to workspaces

citations.claim: pkg.go.dev indexes public modules fetched through the official proxy and exposes importer/consumer graphs, aiding ecosystem discoverability.
citations.support: For public modules, it indexes which packages import a given package and shows an importer list.

citations.claim: This discoverability proxy has a stated limitation: it only covers public modules reachable through the public proxy, not private or internally-hosted modules.
citations.support: The limitation is sharp: pkg.go.dev only indexes public modules fetched through the public Go module proxy at proxy.golang.org.

rubric: D1 (0-20): Native/official package manager integrated into the toolchain
D2 (0-20): Reproducibility and integrity verification (lockfile-equivalent, checksums)
D3 (0-20): Official registry/proxy infrastructure availability and reliability
D5 (0-20): Declared ecosystem-activity proxy (public module discoverability via the official index), used only as one input alongside the other four dimensions, with stated limitations
metric.package_dependency_management_qua.scoring_rationale: Go scores near-ceiling because module management is fully first-party and integrated into the `go` command with no separate installation (D1=20), and reproducibility/integrity is enforced by default via go.sum plus an independently auditable, cryptographically tamper-evident checksum database since Go 1.13 (D2=20). D3 is capped slightly below 20 because reliability of the official proxy/index/checksum trio is well documented but represents centralized Google-operated infrastructure rather than a fully decentralized guarantee. D4 is capped further because multi-module workspace support (go.work, introduced Go 1.18) and workspace vendoring are functional and actively maintained but have documented edge-case friction between per-module and per-workspace vendoring. D5 uses the declared proxy-index discoverability signal only as one of five dimensions, explicitly noting its public-module-only limitation rather than treating it as a standalone popularity metric.

evidence.retrieval_route: web_search tool, official go.dev documentation/release notes, go.dev wiki CodeTools page, Go module proxy/checksum documentation (proxy.golang.org, sum.golang.org), and third-party tooling guides cross-checked against official sources
